Dodge and West Dodge connect residential: Dodge and West Dodge connect residential neighborhoods with shopping, campuses, medical services, and downtown Omaha. Traffic along this east-west corridor reflects trips between these destinations and the streets that feed into it.
A city or county view brings local conne: A city or county view brings local connections into focus: streets linking neighborhoods with jobs, shops, and services. The individual approach volumes provide context for how traffic reaches each crossing; high daily traffic alone does not describe congestion.
I-80 and I-680 link major Omaha streets: I-80 and I-680 link major Omaha streets with regional and longer-distance travel. Multiple high-volume connections along these corridors reflect traffic gathering at ramps and other links across the highway network, rather than at a single street crossing.
At the city or county scale, ramps conne: At the city or county scale, ramps connect surrounding roads with through routes. These connections serve nearby destinations as well as longer-distance trips. Directional leg volumes help distinguish the approaches contributing to an interchange's total daily traffic.
Estimated regional travel increased abou: Estimated regional travel increased about 5% from 2022 to 2025. Douglas County grew 6.5%, Sarpy County 6.2%, and Pottawattamie and Mills counties 2.3%. District maps show where that growth occurred.
Vehicle miles traveled combines road len: Vehicle miles traveled combines road length and traffic volume. A methodology change between 2022 and 2023 introduced the OSM network and broader local-road coverage. Centerline miles and directional network miles are different measures; comparisons across that break need care.
Traffic generally rises from late spring: Traffic generally rises from late spring through early fall. Rural interstate counts vary more by season than urban interstate counts. Combined urban counts can hide differences between individual counter locations.
The five monitored Omaha pedestrian loca: The five monitored Omaha pedestrian locations recorded a combined daily average of 1,607 in 2025, down from 2,443 in 2020. Bicycle counts followed a different path. These results describe the monitored locations, not the entire trail network.
Recorded walking, running, and hiking gr: Recorded walking, running, and hiking grew in 2024 and 2025. Strava represents its users rather than all regional activity. Growth in app use can influence the totals; compare these patterns with permanent counter data.
Recorded passenger counts rose after the: Recorded passenger counts rose after the low levels in 2021 and peaked in October 2024. April 2025 remained above April 2024, with ORBT accounting for approximately one in six recorded passenger counts.
Heartland Bike Share operated 80 station: Heartland Bike Share operated 80 stations in 2025. The Bob Kerrey Pedestrian Bridge had the highest station activity. Omaha recorded 373,541 scooter trips, concentrated in the warmer months; monthly totals do not isolate event-related travel.

Six of seven roadway classes recorded VM: Six of seven roadway classes recorded VMT growth in 2024-2025. Local roads had the largest rebound, rising 8.3% after a 5.1% decline in 2023-2024. Principal arterials returned to growth (+1.9%), while freeways and both collector classes posted stronger gains. Interstate travel was nearly unchanged (+0.1%); minor arterials remained down 1.5%.
Ten of the 15 active counters have count: Ten of the 15 active counters have counted continuously since 1994, providing a consistent set of sites for long-term traffic comparisons. These locations are highlighted and labeled in the table: Iowa 914 and Nebraska A-5, A-17, A-23, A-24, A-25, A-26, A-32, A-40, and A-56.

The heat map is weighted by 2025 interse: The heat map is weighted by 2025 intersection traffic volumes. Stronger colors highlight areas with more daily vehicle activity.
Annual average daily traffic shows how m: Annual average daily traffic shows how many vehicles use an intersection. It does not measure delay or peak-hour queues.
Most Metro stops showed higher passenger: Most Metro stops showed higher passenger activity per 100 scheduled visits between April 2022 and April 2025.
The largest gain was at 35th & Broadway: The largest gain was at 35th & Broadway in Council Bluffs: +430 passenger activities per 100 scheduled visits. Other large gains included 22nd & Cuming SE (+345), Westroads ORBT (+269), and 153rd & Weir Park & Ride NW (+261).
Stop productivity fell at all stops alon: Stop productivity fell at all stops along Farnam as Metro rerouted fixed-route service to avoid streetcar construction.
Sarpy was the only subregion with VMT gr: Sarpy was the only subregion with VMT growth each year from 2022 through 2025. Growth slowed to 0.4% in 2024, then reached 2.4% in 2025. Outer Douglas and Pottawattamie recorded small declines in 2024 before returning to growth in 2025.
Urban core VMT rose 7.8% in 2023, then d: Urban core VMT rose 7.8% in 2023, then declined 1.4% in 2024 and 0.5% in 2025. By 2025 it remained slightly below its 2023 level. Construction and changes in commuting are possible influences, but their effects were not measured.
Principal arterial counts recovered afte: Principal arterial counts recovered after spring 2020 and generally rose after 2022. In 2025, monthly average daily traffic exceeded earlier years except in February and March. The busiest period was typically late spring through early fall, with lower volumes toward year-end.
Development around Gretna may help expla: Development around Gretna may help explain increased traffic on US 6 between western Omaha and I-80. US 75 pavement and bridge repairs through Bellevue began in August 2024, with overnight lane and ramp closures that may have shifted trips.
Counts on 16th Street in Council Bluffs: Counts on 16th Street in Council Bluffs recovered in 2021 and stayed generally higher in 2022 and 2023. Nearby I-29 reconstruction brought phased closures from late 2021; both directions reopened in August 2023. Lower counts in 2024 and 2025 may partly reflect traffic returning to I-29 rather than a sustained decline in travel.

I-80 west of the Gretna interchange carr: I-80 west of the Gretna interchange carries its highest traffic from May through October and lighter volumes in winter. Vacation and recreational trips may contribute to this seasonal difference.
Monthly counts have changed little since: Monthly counts have changed little since 2022. Although 2025 was among the highest years shown, especially in January and late spring, recent-year differences were generally small. The winter-to-summer swing is more pronounced than year-to-year growth at this site.
Combined I-80, I-680, and I-480 counts w: Combined I-80, I-680, and I-480 counts were generally higher in 2024 and 2025 than in 2022 and 2023, but increases were small. The highest combined volumes in 2025 occurred in June and October, with little change between those months.
Urban interstate counts vary less by sea: Urban interstate counts vary less by season than the rural I-80 site west of Gretna. Regular commuting may contribute to the steadier pattern, but the combined totals can mask different trends at individual I-80, I-680, and I-480 counters.
Preliminary statewide ATR totals through: Preliminary statewide ATR totals through December 2025 showed cumulative traffic growth of 1.2% in Nebraska and 0.19% in Iowa compared with 2024. Nebraska recorded much higher January volumes, while both states had substantial monthly declines in February.
The series sums annual AADT at the ten c: The series sums annual AADT at the ten counters operating continuously since 1994. Their combined daily traffic rose over the long term, dropped sharply in 2020, and recovered above its pre-2020 peak by 2025. These sites cover urban and rural interstates, highways, and a municipal street in Iowa and Nebraska.
Annual regional VMT averaged 0.6% growth: Annual regional VMT averaged 0.6% growth from 2022 to 2025, below the earlier 1% safety-planning assumption. The 2026-2028 estimates apply that observed 0.6% annual rate to illustrate possible future growth. Values through 2025 are historic totals; later years are projections, not observed traffic.
Average daily pedestrian counts at five: Average daily pedestrian counts at five monitored Omaha locations fell each year, from a combined 2,443 in 2020 to 1,607 in 2025, a decrease of about 34%.
The western approach to the Bob Kerrey P: The western approach to the Bob Kerrey Pedestrian Bridge remained the busiest pedestrian location from 2020 through 2025.
The combined daily average fell from 1,1: The combined daily average fell from 1,122 in 2020 to 665 in 2022, then rose in 2023 and 2024. The 2025 average of 684 was about 13% below 2024 but slightly above 2022.
National bicycle counts in 2023 fell 2.1: National bicycle counts in 2023 fell 2.1% on recreational facilities and rose 6.9% on commuter routes.
Recorded running, walking, and hiking ro: Recorded running, walking, and hiking rose substantially in 2024 and 2025. Monthly activities peaked at approximately 73,000 in August 2025, compared with about 55,000 in September 2024. The largest year-to-year differences occurred from late spring through early fall.
Strava flagged approximately 15% of regi: Strava flagged approximately 15% of regional activities as commutes in 2025; most were recreational. Its totals represent participating users, not all regional walking or running trips.
The highest monthly bicycle count was ap: The highest monthly bicycle count was approximately 20,000 activities in July 2020. Summer peaks from 2021 through 2025 were generally 15,000-16,000. Cycling rose through spring and declined after summer each year, without the large recent increases seen in running, walking, and hiking.
Douglas had the largest county totals, r: Douglas had the largest county totals, reaching approximately 59,000 recorded activities in August 2025. Its highest summer activity levels occurred in 2025, following increases in 2024.
Sarpy reached approximately 21,000 recor: Sarpy reached approximately 21,000 recorded activities in August 2025, its highest summer level after gains in 2024. Gretna Crossing Park opened in September 2023 with walking and bicycle trails, adding places to be active.
Pottawattamie reached approximately 7,40: Pottawattamie reached approximately 7,400 recorded activities in September 2025. Like Douglas and Sarpy, it recorded its highest summer activity levels in 2025 after increases in 2024. The FIRST AVE trail in Council Bluffs opened in stages during this period.
Recorded passenger counts rose after the: Recorded passenger counts rose after the low levels in 2021, reaching their highest count in October 2024. April 2025 was below that peak but remained above April 2024.
ORBT accounted for approximately one in: ORBT accounted for approximately one in six recorded passenger counts in April 2025.
Heartland Bike Share has operated in the: Heartland Bike Share has operated in the Omaha metro since 2011. Rider activity received a boost following the pandemic and continued to increase through 2025.
Omaha recorded 373,541 scooter trips in: Omaha recorded 373,541 scooter trips in 2025, primarily in Downtown, Midtown, Aksarben, and Benson. Across 2020-2025, the highest combined monthly total occurred in June. Use stayed relatively high from July through September before falling in autumn and winter.

Traffic Analysis Districts (TAD) are are: Traffic Analysis Districts (TAD) are areas bounded by major roads. They help compare traffic across urban, suburban, and outlying neighborhoods.
For the first time, traffic estimates co: For the first time, traffic estimates cover all roads, including local streets, using data from StreetLight Insight planning tools.
StreetLight estimates were adjusted usin: StreetLight estimates were adjusted using short-duration and continuous traffic counts. Where enough counts were available, adjustment factors were calculated for each Federal Functional Classification (FFC) within a TAD. Regional factors were used where local counts were limited.
Adjusted volumes were checked for consis: Adjusted volumes were checked for consistency along corridors and across years, considering travel direction, divided roadways, and traffic entering or leaving intersections. Observed counts took priority when resolving differences.
Vehicle miles traveled combines the numb: Vehicle miles traveled combines the number of vehicles with the distance they travel; district values on the map are shown in thousands.
The transition from the legacy Traffic F: The transition from the legacy Traffic Flow centerline network to the Metropolitan Area Transportation Systems (MATS) network, built on OpenStreetMap (OSM), changed the methodology and affects comparisons with earlier VMT estimates.
For the 2022-2025 comparison, the 2022 a: For the 2022-2025 comparison, the 2022 average daily VMT baseline was backcast by dividing 2023 average daily VMT by 1.055. This uses the regional median growth rate of 5.5% across stable Traffic Analysis Districts (TAD) between 2022 and 2023.
The harmonized baseline reduces the infl: The harmonized baseline reduces the influence of differences in network representation on the reported trend.
Western Douglas and southwestern Sarpy h: Western Douglas and southwestern Sarpy had some of the largest increases. Several districts grew by more than 10% between 2022 and 2025.
Some central Omaha districts declined wh: Some central Omaha districts declined while the urban core grew overall. Temporary street restrictions may have moved trips to nearby roads.
District totals show where travel change: District totals show where travel changed. They do not separate the effects of construction, development, or changes in commuting.
Travel rose 6.5% in Douglas, 6.2% in Sar: Travel rose 6.5% in Douglas, 6.2% in Sarpy, and 2.3% across Pottawattamie and Mills between 2022 and 2025.
Some central Omaha districts saw decline: Some central Omaha districts saw declines even as the urban core grew overall. Construction may have shifted routes; its effect was not measured.
Interstates and freeways move traffic ov: Interstates and freeways move traffic over longer distances. Local streets provide more direct access to homes and businesses.

The 2023 method includes more local road: The 2023 method includes more local roads and counts each travel direction. Comparisons across 2022-2023 are not like-for-like.
Continuous traffic counters capture dail: Continuous traffic counters capture daily changes instead of a single short survey. The counter inventory lists 15 regional sites. Ten have counted continuously since 1994, providing a long-term record across urban and rural interstates, highways, and a municipal street.
A regional total can hide differences be: A regional total can hide differences between individual roads. Counter locations give those trends a geographic context.
Traffic generally rises from late spring: Traffic generally rises from late spring through early fall. Rural interstate travel varies more by season than urban interstate travel.
Year-to-year lines make seasonal changes: Year-to-year lines make seasonal changes easier to separate from longer-term changes in traffic.
MAPA, the City of Omaha, THOR (Trails Ha: MAPA, the City of Omaha, THOR (Trails Have Our Respect), and Fontenelle Forest partner to operate bicycle and pedestrian counters across the region.
Permanent counters track bicycle and ped: Permanent counters track bicycle and pedestrian activity on regional trails. MAPA has installed counters since 2016 and expanded the network to better represent the regional trail system.
Trail-use analysis uses Eco-Counter data: Trail-use analysis uses Eco-Counter data from City of Omaha locations only, adjusted for counter failures and weather conditions. These sites do not measure every walking or cycling trip in the metro.
ORBT connects Westroads Mall with downto: ORBT connects Westroads Mall with downtown Omaha along Dodge and Douglas Streets. Buses arrive every 10 minutes during most weekday daytime hours. Raised platforms, three-door boarding, and arrival displays support the route's stations.
ORBT opened in November 2020 and reached: ORBT opened in November 2020 and reached two million rides by its fourth anniversary in November 2024. It accounted for approximately one in six recorded passenger counts in April 2025.
Stop productivity was highest in the urb: Stop productivity was highest in the urban core and at Westroads, Metro College, and North Omaha Transit Centers.
North Omaha Transit Center averaged 406: North Omaha Transit Center averaged 406 passenger activities per 100 scheduled visits across its 12 bays in April 2025.

Stop productivity was lowest along the s: Stop productivity was lowest along the southern and northwestern edges of Metro's service area, where routes often operated as express services or at lower frequencies than in the urban core.
The 2025 network had 80 stations. The Bo: The 2025 network had 80 stations. The Bob Kerrey Pedestrian Bridge led station activity; Downtown, Midtown, and Aksarben were also higher-activity areas. Newer stations at Chalco Hills and Twin Creek in Bellevue were well used.
Omaha's 2025 scooter trips were concentr: Omaha's 2025 scooter trips were concentrated in warmer months. Monthly totals do not separate travel tied to specific events.
